skill_traces.query:
Nate: Hey Joanna, what's been up since we last chatted? How's it going?
Joanna: Hey Nate! Another movie script that I contributed to was shown on the big screen last Sunday for the first time! It was such a surreal experience to see everything come together. I felt a mix of emotions, but overall, it was a satisfying moment. I've been waiting for this for a long time!
Nate: Congrats Joanna! How was it to finally see it on the big screen?

[shares a photo holding a videogame controller]
Joanna: It was an amazing experience! I'll never forget seeing all of the characters and dialogue I wrote being acted out - it was such a cool feeling. Having all the hard work and determination I put into writing pay off was definitely rewarding. I know this is the third time it's happened, but its just so awesome!
Nate: That must have been amazing. What was your favorite part of it?
Joanna: Seeing my characters I worked so hard on come alive was my favorite part. It felt like they jumped off the page and became real - it was totally surreal.
Nate: Wow Joanna, those drawings are really incredible! What inspired you to create them?
Joanna: Thanks, Nate! They're visuals of the characters to help bring them alive in my head so I can write better.
Nate: That's a cool way to gain insight into your characters. Where did you get your ideas for them?
Joanna: I got ideas from everywhere: people I know, stuff I saw, even what I imagined. It's cool to see how an idea takes shape into a person with their own wants, worries, and wishes.
Nate: Wow Joanna, that's so cool! It's amazing how our imaginations can bring ideas to life. Can you tell me more about the character on the left in the photo?
Joanna: Nope! You'll just have to watch the movie and find out for yourself!
Nate: You got it. I was already planning on watching it, but talking to you about it makes me want to watch it even more!
Joanna: Awesome! Well enough about me, what have you been up to?
Nate: I was bored today, so I just took my turtles out for a walk.
Joanna: Sound fun! Did they have a good time?
Nate: Of course! They look tired from all the walking, so they're relaxing in the tank right now.
Joanna: Aww, they're so cute! What do they eat?
Nate: They eat a combination of vegetables, fruits, and insects. They have a varied diet.
Joanna: Wow, that's fascinating! It's interesting how they have such a varied diet, including insects. Do you have a favorite among their food choices?
Nate: I love seeing them eat fruit - they get so hyped and it's so cute!
Joanna: Wow, that's so cute! They look like they really enjoy fruit.
Nate: Yeah, it's adorable! Watching them enjoy their favorite snacks is so fun. I also like holding them.
Joanna: Do they have different personalities, like the way dogs and cats do?
Nate: Yeah, they each do. One is more adventurous while the other is more reserved, which I find cute. Having them around brings me joy and they make great companions.
Joanna: That's super cool! I never knew turtles could be so interesting until I met your turtles. Wow!
Nate: I've always liked turtles since I was a boy, so I know all about them!
Joanna: You'll have to keep me posted on them! It's been fun chatting!
Nate: See you later Joanna!

selected.name: Extract Comfort and Joy Sources
selected.description: Use when a message states that something cheers the user up, brings joy, or provides comfort.
content: During extraction, if the user mentions a pet, hobby, person, item, or activity that provides cheer, comfort, or emotional support, create a separate durable memory (preference, relationship, or state) capturing that source, even when the message also contains stress or negative events.
Do not merge the supportive source only into a negative-event candidate; it should be its own candidate so it survives later SKIP/MERGE decisions.
Extract only sources explicitly stated as supportive; do not infer unmentioned ones.
selected.rerank_reason: Joanna mentions her turtles as sources of comfort and joy, which aligns with the skill's purpose of identifying comfort and joy sources.

nearby_not_selected.name: Capture Brief Project Mentions with Full Attributes
nearby_not_selected.description: Use when a speaker mentions a project they completed, are working on, or plan to build, even briefly.
content: Create an event candidate for any explicit statement of a completed, ongoing, or planned project, even in small talk.
When several messages describe the same project, consolidate them into one candidate and include every explicit attribute stated.
Stop once the speaker has finished describing the project in that session.

nearby_not_selected.name: Capture likely deceased from euphemistic absence language
nearby_not_selected.description: During extraction, when a speaker describes someone with euphemistic absence language (e.g., 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him/her here') that strongly implies death, use this guidance.
content: When a statement euphemistically implies a person has died without explicitly saying so, also extract the implied state that the person is likely deceased, in addition to the literal statement.
Record the inference with an appropriate hedge (e.g., 'likely deceased') because the speaker did not state it directly; do not assert cause, date, or circumstances of death.
Stop after capturing the likely-deceased state and the literal content; do not extrapolate further details about the person or the relationship.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Origin Events as Distinct Memories
nearby_not_selected.description: When a user explains how they started or got into an activity, hobby, or interest, including who introduced it or when it began.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an origin narrative (how the person started an activity, who introduced it, what prompted it, or a concrete start time), create a separate event memory for the origin in addition to any preference or state memory.
Record the causal source (person or circumstance) and the start time/age if stated; do not fold the origin into a generic preference summary.
If the origin names another person, also consider a relationship memory capturing that connection.
Emit at most one origin memory per activity per message; skip if the same origin is repeated later.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract Explicit Preference Statements
nearby_not_selected.description: When a speaker explicitly states a preference, favorite, or strong like/dislike for a specific item or activity, create a preference memory during extraction.
content: During extraction, scan every message for explicit preference expressions (e.g., 'I love', 'my favorite is', 'really into', 'X is beautiful', 'go crazy for') and create a preference candidate for each distinct item or activity mentioned.
Include preferences attributed to the speaker's pets, children, or family as valid memories; record the specific subject and the liked items/activities.
Do not convert explicit enjoyment into a recommendation or event memory; preserve the original preference wording.
Capture preferences from casual, short, or reflective statements, including those with positive affect (e.g., 'awesome', 'so fun') even without 'I like'.
Stop after capturing all explicit preferences; do not infer additional ones beyond what is stated.

nearby_not_selected.name: Preserve Specific Plan Details in Event Memory Extraction
nearby_not_selected.description: When extracting an event or plan memory and messages state what participants will try, do, or consume, include those concrete details in the memory content.
content: During extraction of event/plan memories, if messages explicitly state what participants will try, do, or consume (e.g., a specific dish, drink, or activity), preserve those concrete items in the memory content instead of replacing them with a generic label like 'date' or 'meet up'.
When the same plan is mentioned across multiple messages, merge the explicitly stated specifics into one memory record, but do not add details that were not said.
